text: The work is hauling other people through town on foot, and Matsugoro is the man everyone is glad to see doing it. He is poor. He is also the most agreeable person in the neighborhood, which in his position amounts to a second job. Then a boy named Toshio is hurt, Matsugoro helps him, and the boy's parents take him on — the hinge the whole picture turns on, a street fixture brought inside a household where he will always be the help. Hiroshi Inagaki takes eighty minutes over it, and the action-adventure filing is a poor description of what fills them. The year is 1943, worth holding in mind while a Japanese studio spends its attention on a cart puller's affections and on the exact distance a household keeps from a man it likes.

Two hours and seven minutes is a long stretch to spend beside a reporter whose beat is celebrity filler. He works in television's lower registers, chasing whatever will fill a segment, and then a thread comes loose: pensions, a pitch built on gold prices, ordinary savings moving somewhere they will not come back from. The scam is the kind that needs paperwork and patience rather than nerve. Yojiro Takita does not turn this into a thriller. The joke and the injury stay in the same room, which is harder to sit with. Japan, 1986. The reporter's difficulty is not danger; it is that he has been paid for years to look away, and the one story that would require him to look is now in his hands, worth less to his employers than his last piece of nonsense.

The umbrellas get made and the money goes somewhere else, on things the maker cannot afford and buys anyway. His debts do not stay his own. They arrive at his daughter, who has a suitor she does not want and a father starting to price her against what he owes. Masahiro Makino stages this as a musical — period dress, songs, sixty-nine minutes — and the combination is the entire proposition. A story about a man weighing what his child is worth, taken at the pitch of light comedy, in Japan in 1939. The songs do not soften the arithmetic. They keep it moving, which turns out to be a stranger effect and a more useful one, since nobody in the film is given the time to arrange a defense of himself.

Saburo and Keiko fall in love on a schedule other people are setting. The war separates them, and the film's own date — 1950 — puts it near enough to the event that its first audiences would have needed nothing explained: the letters, the waiting, the sense of a life being administered from somewhere else. Tadashi Imai gives it a hundred and eleven minutes and declines to make the couple exceptional. That is the choice worth noticing. A war picture organized around campaigns has a shape ready-made; this one has two people trying to stay a couple while decisions taken far above them keep moving the furniture. Imai's attention stays on small logistics — where to meet, how long there is, who has to leave first — and the tenderness in it is largely a matter of scheduling.

He went to prison so the gang would not have to, and by the time he is out the gang has decided he was always too much. Kinji Fukasaku shot it at eighty-six minutes, and the shape of it is a man discovering that his trade was reorganized while he was inside: same streets, same names, a new arithmetic of who is worth keeping. The two men he falls in with are called brothers, a word that in this line means obligation rather than blood. Violence here is not stylized into something admirable. It is the labor, and the labor has been handed to people who do less of it. He tries for a life on the other side of that. What he is trying to leave was never built with an exit, and the film is cold about how much of his own decision-making was ever his.

Three swordsmen sell their services to whichever lord will fill a rice bowl, and they enter every house through the servants' door. They also hold themselves to a code that the arrangement makes absurd: men for hire who believe they belong to something. Kon Ichikawa keeps the comedy and the seriousness in one frame for a hundred minutes and lets neither win, which is uncomfortable by design. Feudal Japan is here as a labor market — hunger, a day's work, a lord with money this month and none the next. The Kinema Junpo All-Time Best Japanese Films list has room for it, and ten minutes with these three suggests why: the talk is small, the grievances are exact, and the walking between jobs is most of the life.

The classmate they set out to rescue is the one who has been making their lives miserable. Three high-school students go looking for a kidnapped bully, and the search takes them past yakuza who cannot be bothered and police who are worse. A hundred and eighteen minutes for an errand this size is an argument in itself: Shinji Sōmai would rather follow the three of them than move them anywhere. The adults are obstacles the way weather is an obstacle, present and uninterested. What the children are really doing, once the pretext is set, is spending days outside school among people who have no use for them. Crime and comedy are both accurate labels, and neither prepares anyone for how much of this is riding, waiting, and watching the next plan come apart.

Tetsuo has a working theory about rich people, and then he meets one it does not survive. Chika's family has money and his has none, and Kichitaro Negishi spends eighty-five minutes on what that does to two people who would otherwise be uncomplicated about each other. The difference operates as pressure rather than as a lesson: which houses can be entered, whose time is free, who has to be somewhere by six. A thriller tag sits on the record beside romance and drama, and it is the one worth taking seriously — the tension in this is not only between the two of them. 1981. Negishi neither cures Tetsuo of his distrust nor makes him charming about it, and the film is better for leaving it intact.

Oryu is looking for a blind child she left behind, and the search drops her into somebody else's war over territory. Tai Katō sets much of the fighting in and around a Tokyo theater — a building with an audience, a stage, and back doors that people in her trade use for other purposes. The setting does work: a place built for spectators, borrowed for a fight none of them agreed to watch. Two obligations, and they do not fit into the same day. One is private and years old. The other belongs to an organization that expects formality, exactness and availability from a woman who gambles for its money. The film keeps the cost of moving between them in view, which is the more interesting of the two wars.

It is August, school is nearly over, and nobody in the group has anything they are required to do. Toshiya Fujita gives ninety-one minutes to a set of high-school friends in the last summer they will share — sex, idleness, the specific tedium of waiting out a deadline none of them set. The method is closer to duration than to plot. Days pass, and the film trusts that what they cost will register without being announced. Japan, 1971, and the freedom on screen is real freedom, which is why it turns uneasy: nothing to push against, no adult in the frame worth defying, only time going by at its own rate. The end of summer is not an event anyone here can schedule. It arrives the way the season does, and every one of them knows the date without saying it.

The arrangement is simple: a law student is paid to teach an undergraduate, an hour at a time. He plays football, he has a career already sketched for him by people who arrange such things, and she occupies a lower rung of the same institution. The romance that grows out of the sessions inherits that asymmetry instead of escaping it. Tatsumi Kumashiro is unsentimental about the setup. Whatever goes wrong is not sprung on anyone; it is legible from the first hour, in who sets the schedule and who is paid. Japan in 1974, eighty-five minutes, and ambition here is neither virtue nor vice but a way of handling a person who has less of it. The film watches him do it and keeps watching after it stops being flattering.

A cold spell threatened the harvest, and a crew already filming in the valley below went up the mountain to look. Shinsuke Ogawa's company stayed. What began as an inquiry into weather and soil — the film borrows the manners of a science lesson, measuring what a bad season does to rice — turns into the life history of the village itself. Two hundred and ten minutes is a demand, and it is also the only unit of time in which a settlement this small can talk at its own pace. The war is still in the room, decades on. The children have gone to the cities, and the arithmetic of who is left to work the fields needs no narrator. Ogawa filmed from the top of the country and kept the whole of it in view.

By 1970 the student movements had reached the high schools, and this one takes its subject from there. He is not a leader of anything. Eighty-nine minutes are given to a task harder than politics: making himself apply, to work, to thought, to a life that asks something of him instead of the comfortable one he already has. Shirō Moritani keeps the scale small, so the movements stay in the background like weather. What happens is internal and gradual, mostly a boy arguing himself into effort while a great many people his age are busy arguing with the state. The two scales do not cancel each other out. They sit side by side for the length of the film, and the private one is the harder to win.

A bank scandal is not a crime scene anyone can photograph, and a detective has been assigned to one anyway. There is no moment of the deed to reconstruct and no weapon to trace — only ledgers, positions, and men in no hurry to be interviewed. Ninety-eight minutes, 1971, directed by Shintarō Katsu. The pressure on the investigator is institutional patience: an organization that can outwait one man has won most of the argument before he starts. Corruption of this kind is slow, procedural and well defended, and a police story built on it has to find its pace somewhere other than pursuit. What it has instead is the arrangement — one man with a mandate, inside a building full of people who work there and have reasons to be unhelpful.
